tips.title: Binary search needs a sorted list
tips.body: Linear search works on **any** list. Binary search only works on a list that is **already in order**, because every step assumes that everything left of the midpoint is smaller. Saying so is the single most examined fact about the two.

tips.title: Halve, compare, discard
tips.body: Binary search is three moves repeated: go to the **middle**, compare it with the target, and **throw away the half that cannot contain it**. Naming the discarded half in your answer is what shows you understand it, rather than just knowing the word.

tips.title: Count the items examined, not the loops
tips.body: When a question asks how many items are **checked**, count the values actually compared with the target. For the list in this topic, finding 23 takes **6** by linear search and **3** by binary — and the 3 is the answer, not the number of times round the loop.

tips.title: Doubling the list adds one step
tips.body: Every extra step of binary search **doubles** the list it can handle. So going from 1000 items to 2000 adds a **single** step, where linear search does twice the work. That is the comparison an efficiency question wants.

tips.title: Both must stop when it is not there
tips.body: Linear search stops at the **end of the list**. Binary search stops when the **range is empty** — when the low end passes the high end. An algorithm that never reports failure is wrong, and it is a common thing to leave out.

why.matters:
Two algorithms that do exactly the same job, and one of them is unimaginably faster on a large list. That is the whole point of comparing them: **how** an algorithm works decides what it can be used on.

It also introduces the one trade that never goes away. Binary search is faster and needs the list **sorted** first; linear search works on anything. Which is better depends on how often you search and how often the list changes, and that is a question about the situation rather than the code.

examples.title: Why a phone book never needed an index
examples.body:
Looking for a name in a sorted book  nobody starts at page one. You open it in the middle  see which half the name is in  and throw the other half away — and then do it again.

Each step halves what is left  so a list of 1 000 takes about **10** checks instead of 1 000. A list of a million takes **20**  and a billion takes **30**. Multiplying the list by a thousand adds **ten** checks  which is why binary search is the reason searching enormous collections feels instant.

visual.alt: A table of the worst case for each search: a thousand items needs a thousand checks by linear search and ten by binary, a million needs a million or twenty, and a billion needs a billion or thirty

examples.title: Why the faster one is not always the right one
examples.body:
Binary search only works on a **sorted** list, and sorting is not free. If the list arrives unsorted and you search it once, sorting it first costs far more than simply looking through it.

The sums change completely if you search it a thousand times, or if it is already sorted because it is kept that way. So the question is never *which algorithm is faster* — it is what the list is like and what you are going to do with it. That is the reasoning an exam question about choosing an algorithm wants to see.

visual.alt: A table comparing linear and binary search: linear needs no sorting and is slow on a huge list, binary needs a sorted list and is fast, so an unsorted list searched once is a case for linear search

examples.title: Why halving beats speeding up
examples.body:
A faster computer makes linear search faster by whatever factor the machine improved. It does not change the **shape** of the problem: ten times the list still takes ten times as long.

Binary search changes the shape. Ten times the list adds about three checks, and a thousand times adds ten. That is why choosing the algorithm matters more than buying hardware, and it is the first case in the course of something that happens repeatedly: the way a method scales beats how fast each step is.

steps.title: Two ways to find something
steps.body:
**A search algorithm looks for one value in a list.** The specification names two, and expects you to explain how each works, and to compare them.

**Linear search** starts at the beginning and checks every item in turn until it finds the target or runs out of list. It makes **no assumption** about the order, which is its strength: it works on any list at all.

**Binary search** repeatedly looks at the **middle** item, and throws away the half that cannot contain the target. It is far quicker, but it carries one hard condition:

> **Binary search only works on a list that is already sorted.**

That condition is the most examined fact in the topic. Everything binary search does depends on it: if the list is not in order, "everything to the left is smaller" is false, and discarding half the list throws away the answer.

**Both must be able to fail.** A search for something that is not there has to finish and report that. Linear search finishes when it reaches the end; binary search finishes when the range it is searching becomes empty.

visuals.alt: A four-box comparison of linear and binary search, how each works and how each finishes when the value is absent

steps.title: Binary search, step by step
steps.body:
**Keep track of the range you are still searching**, as a low position and a high position. The midpoint is the item halfway between them.

At each step: compare the midpoint with the target. If it matches, stop. If the midpoint is **too small**, the target must be to the **right**, so the low end moves past the midpoint. If it is **too big**, the target is to the **left**, so the high end moves back.

steps.title: When the value is not there
steps.body:
**A search must be able to report failure.** This is the half of the algorithm that gets left out of exam answers, and it is where the marks often are.

Linear search is easy: it stops when it reaches the end of the list without a match.

Binary search stops when the **range becomes empty** — when the low position passes the high position. There is nowhere left that the value could be hiding, because every step only discarded items that could not have held it.

steps.text: Midpoint of 5 and 9 is 7, holding **56**. Too big, so high becomes 6
steps.note: the same two steps as the successful search, because the list is unchanged

steps.text: Midpoint of 5 and 6 is 5, holding **23**. Too small, so low becomes 6
steps.note: the range is now just position 6

steps.text: Midpoint of 6 and 6 is 6, holding **38**. Too small, so low becomes 7
steps.note: low is now greater than high

steps.text: The range is **empty**, so 40 is **not in the list** — reported after 4 items examined
steps.note: linear search would have checked all 10 before reaching the same conclusion

check.prompt: How does binary search know a value is not in the list?
options: The range becomes empty: the low position passes the high position
It reaches the last item of the list
It examines the same midpoint twice in a row
It has halved the list ten times
check.solution: Each step discards only items that **cannot** hold the target, so when the range is empty there is nowhere left to look. Reaching the end of the list is how **linear** search fails, not binary.

steps.title: Comparing them
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to compare and contrast the two, and to explain why one is more efficient.** It also says that **only time efficiency** is examined, and that no formal notation is needed — so the comparison is made in plain words and in counts of items examined.

**Linear search is slower but less demanding.** In the worst case it examines **every** item: for a list of $n$ items, $n$ checks. But it works on **any** list, sorted or not, and needs no preparation.

**Binary search is far quicker but demands a sorted list.** Each step **halves** what is left, so the number of steps grows very slowly:

| items in the list | steps at most |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 4 |
| 1000 | 10 |
| 2000 | 11 |

**Look at the last two rows.** Doubling the list from 1000 to 2000 costs binary search **one** extra step, while linear search does **twice** the work. That single comparison is the clearest way to answer an efficiency question.

**When is linear search the better choice?** When the list is **unsorted** and would have to be sorted first, when the list is **very short**, or when items are being added and removed constantly so that keeping it sorted costs more than it saves.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say why the sorted condition matters, not just that it exists.** Anyone can write *binary search needs a sorted list*. A top answer says what breaks: the algorithm discards a half on the strength of *everything to the left is smaller*, and in an unsorted list that claim is false, so the discarded half may hold the target and the search reports **not found** when the value is there.

**Count items examined, not iterations.** An efficiency question asks how many **comparisons with the target** are made. Finding 23 in the list above takes **3** for binary search and **6** for linear. Answering with the number of loops, or with the length of the list, misses the point being tested.

**Give the doubling comparison.** *Binary search is faster* is worth little. **Doubling the list adds one step to binary search and doubles the work for linear search** is the comparison that earns the marks, and it is exactly what "compare the efficiency" is asking for.

**Do not overclaim.** Binary search is not always better. Sorting an unsorted list first costs more than a single linear search, and on a handful of items the difference is nothing. A question asking *which would you use* wants the **condition of the data**, not a blanket answer.

**Handle failure explicitly.** Describe how each search **terminates when the value is absent** — linear at the end of the list, binary when the range empties. An algorithm with no stopping condition loops forever, and the specification asks for the mechanics of the algorithm, which includes this.

**The specification limits the comparison.** It says explicitly that **only time efficiency** is examined and that **formal comparisons are not required**. So there is no need for big-O notation, and no marks for it; counts of items examined and clear English are what is wanted.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Linear search** checks every item in turn, from the start, until it finds the target or reaches the end.
- It works on **any** list, sorted or not, and needs no preparation.
- **Binary search** examines the **middle** item and discards the half that cannot hold the target.
- **Binary search only works on a sorted list** — the most examined fact in the topic.
- Why: discarding a half assumes everything to the left is smaller, which is false if unsorted.
- Each step: compare the midpoint, then move **low** past it or **high** back before it.
- Finding 23 in 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91 takes **3** items by binary search and **6** by linear.
- **Linear search fails** by reaching the end of the list.
- **Binary search fails** when the range becomes **empty**, with low past high.
- Worst case: linear examines **n** items; binary examines about **log₂ n**.
- 1000 items takes at most **10** steps; 2000 takes **11**.
- **Doubling the list adds one step to binary and doubles the work for linear.**
- Linear is the better choice on a **short** or **unsorted** list, or one that changes constantly.
- Count **items compared with the target**, not loops.
- The specification examines **time efficiency only**, and asks for **no formal notation**.

questions.prompt: Explain how binary search works, why it requires a sorted list, and how it compares with linear search for efficiency.
questions.solution:
Binary search finds a value in a **sorted** list by repeatedly halving the part of the list still worth searching.

It keeps track of the range under consideration, as a **low** position and a **high** position, starting at the two ends of the list. At each step it examines the item at the **midpoint** of that range and compares it with the target.

If the midpoint **matches**, the search is over. If the midpoint is **smaller** than the target, the target can only lie to the **right**, so the low position moves to just past the midpoint. If the midpoint is **larger**, the target can only lie to the **left**, so the high position moves to just before it. Either way, **half of what was left is discarded in a single step**, and the process repeats on the half that remains.

Searching 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91 for 23 shows it: the midpoint is 16, which is too small, so everything up to it goes; the new midpoint is 56, too big, so everything from it rightwards goes; the next midpoint is 23 itself. **Three** items examined.

The search finishes without a match when the **range becomes empty** — when the low position passes the high position. Every step discarded only items that could not have held the target, so if nothing is left, the value was never there.

**The sorted condition is essential, and the reason is worth stating precisely.** Discarding a half rests entirely on the claim that *everything to the left of the midpoint is smaller and everything to the right is larger*. That claim is only true of a **sorted** list. In an unsorted list the target might sit in the half being thrown away, and the algorithm would confidently report that the value is not present when it is. It is not that binary search runs slowly on unsorted data — it returns the **wrong answer**.

**On efficiency**, linear search examines every item in the worst case: $n$ checks for a list of $n$ items. Binary search halves the range each time, so it needs about $\log_2 n$ checks — at most 10 for 1000 items, and about 20 for a million.

The sharpest way to put the comparison is what happens when the list **doubles**. Going from 1000 items to 2000 costs binary search a **single extra step**, because one more halving covers twice as much; linear search does **twice the work**. Note, though, that binary search is not always the better choice: if the list is unsorted, sorting it first costs more than one pass of linear search, so for a single search of unordered data linear search wins.

questions.prompt: A library system stores 5000 book titles in alphabetical order. Explain which search algorithm should be used and why, including what would change if titles were added and removed constantly without keeping the list in order.
questions.solution:
The titles are held **in alphabetical order**, which is exactly the condition binary search requires, so **binary search** is the right choice.

The gain is large. Linear search would examine up to **5000** titles in the worst case, checking each one in turn until it found the match or reached the end. Binary search halves the range at every step, so it needs at most **13** — since $2^{13} = 8192$, which is comfortably more than 5000. Thirteen comparisons against five thousand is the argument for it, and giving those two numbers is what turns *binary search is faster* into an answer worth marks.

It works because alphabetical order is an order like any other: the algorithm can compare the target with the title at the midpoint and know, with certainty, which half the target must be in. Discarding the other half is safe **only** because of that ordering.

**If titles were added and removed constantly without keeping the list in order, the situation reverses.** Binary search could no longer be used at all — not because it would be slow, but because it would be **wrong**. It would discard a half on the assumption that everything to the left comes earlier alphabetically, and in an unordered list that is false, so a title that is present could be reported as missing.

The options would then be to **sort the list before searching**, or to **use linear search**. Which is better depends on how often the system searches. Sorting 5000 titles costs far more than a single pass of linear search, so for one lookup, linear search wins outright. But if the system searches many times between changes, sorting once and then using binary search repeatedly would pay for itself.

The practical answer for a library is to **keep the list sorted as titles are added and removed**, inserting each new title in its correct place rather than at the end. That keeps the cost of maintaining order small and spread out, and preserves the ability to search 5000 titles in 13 comparisons.

examTechnique.body:
Say **how** the algorithm works, not just what it is called: for binary search, examine the middle, compare, and **discard the half that cannot contain the target**.

The sorted condition needs its reason attached. For efficiency, count **items compared with the target**, and reach for the doubling comparison — one extra step against twice the work.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains **why** the sorted condition matters — that discarding a half assumes order, so an unsorted list makes the search return the **wrong answer**, not merely a slow one. It counts **items compared**, and makes the efficiency point with the **doubling** comparison rather than a vague claim of speed. It describes how each search **terminates when the value is absent**, and it refuses to say binary search is always better, weighing the cost of sorting against how many searches will follow.
